newsitem.title: UK: A guilty plea could shroud copper scandal.
newsitem.headline: A guilty plea could shroud copper scandal.

text.p: Any guilty plea by Japanese trader Yasuo Hamanaka in the Sumitomo Corp copper scandal might draw a curtain over the affair, say some legal experts.

Hamanaka's lawyer said on Tuesday that his client now admits that he forged some documents during the time when he ran up trading losses of $2.6 billion in what Sumitomo alleges were unauthorised deals.

If that translated to a guilty plea in court, it might make it harder for investigators in the United States and Britain, for instance, to pursue inquiries to satisfy themselves that no laws were broken by anyone else in the jurisdictions where copper is traded.
"I would see a plea of guilty as choking off part of the expose," said Michael Levi, professor of Criminology at the University of Wales at Cardiff.

"The moment you plead guilty you stop calling for evidence from any of the other parties and it will probably reduce the number of subpoenas unless there are civil actions going on alongside it," Levi said.

For years metals conglomerate Sumitomo had praised Hamanaka, 48, as a money spinning star trader. Traders called him "Mr Five Percent" because of the chunk of the global copper market that he was said to control.
But Sumitomo announced last June it had uncovered a web of deals hidden by Hamanaka that caused the huge losses. Japanese prosecutors raided his suburban home last week and arrested him.
"Presumably he's hoping for leniency on the basis that the Japanese might not be keen for him to throw a lot of mud at Sumitomo," Levi said.
"If he did start slinging mud at Sumitomo, then more stuff might emerge".
Hamanaka did not say if his superiors had known of his actions, his lawyer reported. Sumitomo insists he acted without their knowledge. But that then raised questions about its supervisory practices.
A Hamanaka admission that he forged documents might make it harder to prosecute anyone else on whom regulatory suspicion fell.
"The likeliest is that the defence may take the line that they were just as deceived by forgeries as anyone else," said Leonard Leigh, professor of criminal law at the London School of Economics.

Any damaging testimony by Hamanaka might also be easier for defence lawyers to challenge. It would be easier for a co-defendent to discredit testimony by someone who had been convicted of forgery, Levi said.
Britain's top fraud investigator said again on Tuesday that its inquiry would continue.
"Our investigation continues...We can't go into operational details but we are continuing to liaise with the Japanese," said Ceinwen Jones, spokeswoman for the Serious Fraud Office.
A senior copper trader said he did not think regulators' investigations outside Japan would be much hampered.

"They want to go into this more deeply and are trying to get information independently of Sumitomo by talking to a lot of people in the market, including those who did business with Hamanaka," he said.

UK authorities would be able to request testimony by witnesses abroad. Documents can be obtained to require foreign courts to take evidence for use in British proceedings, Leigh said. "Another possibility is to take evidence through a live television link," he added.
